items.name: Rigid water containers
items.need: Taps can run dry in an outage or a water-main break, and in tall buildings they stop as soon as the pumps lose power, so a household needs drinking water already stored at home.
items.how_to_choose: Water weighs about 8.3 lb a gallon, so size decides whether you can move a container once it is full: a 3.5-gallon brick is about 30 lb, a 5.5-gallon can about 49 lb, a 7-gallon can about 60 lb, a 15-gallon barrel about 125 lb, and a 55-gallon barrel or tank about 480 lb. Cans of 7 gallons or less can be carried to a tap, to a car or down the stairs, and a leak spoils one can and not the whole supply, which is why the picks here are cans. A 30-gallon or 55-gallon barrel or stackable tank holds far more in one spot (two weeks for four people is 56 gallons) and suits a garage or basement with a concrete floor: fill it where it will stay, and plan on a siphon pump and a bung wrench unless it has a spigot. For a household of more than two with that kind of floor, one 55-gallon barrel holds about two weeks of water for four people. No barrel is ranked here yet; if you buy one, keep a few small cans you can carry as well. Measure the spot before you buy, whether it is a closet floor, the gap under a bed or a garage wall. Spread containers along a wall or across several closets rather than in one tall stack, and keep them upright unless the maker says they can lie on their side. Buy food-grade containers made for drinking water, with a screw cap and a vent.

qty.note: Work it out in three steps: the gallons you want stored, less the gallons you already hold as sealed water, divided by the gallons in one purchased pack and rounded up. Example, two adults for 14 days: 28 gallons to store, 6 already held as sealed water, 22 still needed; that is 4 cans of 5.5 gallons (22 gallons), or 4 cans of 7 gallons (28 gallons, so 6 to spare). A two-pack is two containers: a WaterBrick two-pack holds 7 gallons, not 3.5, so the same household needs 4 two-packs, which is 8 bricks. The sealed water you bought for the first 3 days counts toward the 14-day target: keep it and add containers for the rest. Do not buy 14 days of containers on top of it.

items.already_own: Camping water jugs you already own are fine if they are food-grade, have only ever held drinking water, close tightly and do not smell of plastic or mold after washing. Clean and sanitize them before filling. Do not press old milk or juice jugs, or anything that has held chemicals or fuel, into service.

safety_notes.text: Store at least 1 gallon of water per person per day for 3 days, and aim for a 2-week supply if you can. Store more for pregnant or sick people, pets and hot weather.
safety_notes.source_title: How to Create an Emergency Water Supply

safety_notes.text: Plan on at least one gallon per person per day for several days, for drinking and sanitation. In very hot weather the need can double.
safety_notes.source_title: Water

safety_notes.text: Use FDA-approved food-grade water storage containers. If you cannot, pick a container with a tight-closing top, made of durable unbreakable material (not glass), with a narrow neck if possible. Never use a container that has held toxic chemicals such as bleach or pesticides.
safety_notes.source_title: How to Create an Emergency Water Supply

safety_notes.text: For stored water, use thoroughly washed plastic containers such as soft drink bottles, which are the best choice. Never use a container that has held toxic substances.
safety_notes.source_name: FEMA (archived page, Food and Water in an Emergency)
safety_notes.source_title: Food and Water in an Emergency
safety_notes.research_note: Archived FEMA page. The older FEMA and Red Cross booklet also warns against reusing milk jugs, but its PDF could not be opened on 2026-11-14.

safety_notes.text: To sanitize a container: wash it with soap and rinse well. Mix 1 teaspoon of unscented liquid household chlorine bleach (5% to 9% sodium hypochlorite) in 1 quart of water, pour it in, close the container and shake so the mix touches every inside surface. Wait at least 30 seconds, pour it out, let the container air-dry, then fill with clean water and close it tightly.
safety_notes.source_title: How to Create an Emergency Water Supply

safety_notes.text: Replace tap water you stored yourself every 6 months.
safety_notes.source_title: How to Create an Emergency Water Supply

safety_notes.text: Keep stored water somewhere cool (50 to 70 F), out of direct sunlight and away from gasoline, pesticides and other toxic substances. Label each container 'drinking water' with the date you filled it.
safety_notes.source_title: How to Create an Emergency Water Supply

items.research_note: 2026-11-17 open-up pass. Stock is now a flag, not a test: the Rhino-Pak is Standard again (maker still lists it, 'Back in Stock Soon'), the Aqua-Tainer is Budget again, the Scepter military can is the new top pick, and the WaterBrick is the Compact pick. Large storage weighed on merit today, with no size filter. Pages opened: The Prepared 'Best large water barrels and tanks' (https://theprepared.com/homestead/reviews/large-water-barrels-tanks/, by Thomas Gomez, last updated January 10, 2021; staff experience and 12 hours of research, no hands-on test; features the Smart Tank 50 Gallon stackable and the Legacy Premium 30 Gallon barrel, lists the Legacy 15 gal, Augason Farms 55 gal barrel and WaterPrepared 55 and 160 gal tanks without comment; says a 55-gallon tank holds over 440 lb of water, to check the floor, not to set plastic straight on hot concrete near fuel, and to keep a few 5 to 7 gallon cans as well); WaterPrepared's own page (Blue 55 Gallon Water Storage Tank, 22 x 28 x 30 in, stackable, BPA-free, made in USA, $269.00, was $289.00); Legacy Food Storage's pages (the same WaterPrepared 55-gallon tank at $299.00 with a treatment kit, empty weight 20 lb; a 30-gallon stackable tank with spigot; a 15-gallon barrel, 15.7 in across and 21.5 in high, about 125 lb full, with bung wrench and siphon hose; a 5-gallon stackable box, about 40 lb full); Primal Survivor's review of the WaterPrepared 55 (one author, November 18, 2024: sturdy, spigot sits low, hard to drain fully, about 500 lb full); Augason Farms' own site (the 55-gallon barrel kit address is now a 404 and the site lists only an 'Exodus 35 Gallon Water Tank' at $250.00, so its 55-gallon barrel is not on the maker's site today). Saratoga Farms 5-gallon stackables: The Prepared tested and disqualified them (arrived warped, cap ratchet broke, failed the drop test). No 'Lifetime' water barrel page was looked for. Result: no barrel or tank is a pick. The reason is evidence and use, not size: the only hands-on comparative test (The Prepared, ten containers) limits itself to cans and makes a can its top pick; True Prepper's best overall is also a can; no established outlet has run a hands-on test of barrels; and both The Prepared pages say to keep portable cans even beside a tank. A barrel cannot be moved full, and tap water you store yourself is replaced every 6 months, which means draining it. Per gallon a 55-gallon tank ($269, about $4.90 a gallon) costs about the same as the Standard can ($4.00), so it is not a budget choice either. If the editor wants a large-capacity pick shown, the best-supported one is the WaterPrepared 55 Gallon stackable tank (maker page plus The Prepared's list plus Primal Survivor's hands-on review), but that is one small outlet's test. how_to_choose now describes barrels and their weight plainly. Why ours and not True Prepper's Reliance Aqua-Tainer: The Prepared ran crush and drop tests on both cans, and the Aqua-Tainer failed them while the Rhino-Pak passed; the Aqua-Tainer is our Budget pick. Why ours and not Outdoor Life's Igloo 6-Gallon Camping Water Container: Outdoor Life tested for car camping, not for months of storage, and The Prepared disqualified the current Igloo 6-gallon can for its push-pin vent. items.name: Sealed bottled and long-life water
items.need: Factory-sealed water is ready to store the day you buy it and needs no cleaning, filling or treating.
items.how_to_choose: Ordinary supermarket water is the cheapest and works well if you use it and replace it before the date on the bottle. A case of half-liter bottles and a gallon jug do the same job: bottles need no cups and are easy to share or drop in a bag, while a jug pours for cooking and washing and makes the count simple, one jug for each person each day. Long-life emergency water costs far more per gallon; what you pay for is a stated multi-year shelf life and tough small packs that suit a grab bag or a shelf you will not check often. Know the weight before you carry it home: a gallon jug is about 8.5 lb and a 24-bottle case about 27 lb. Keep sealed water in a cool, dark place off the floor of a sunny room.

qty.note: Enough sealed water for the first 3 days: 1 gallon for each person a day. At two weeks, keep it: it counts toward the 14-day total, and your own containers hold the rest.

items.already_own: Any unopened, commercially bottled water you already have counts. Check that the seal is intact and the date has not passed, then add it to your total.

safety_notes.text: Unopened commercially bottled water is the safest and most reliable emergency water supply. Observe the expiration date on store-bought water.
safety_notes.source_title: How to Create an Emergency Water Supply

safety_notes.text: Keep commercially bottled water sealed in its original container and store it in a cool, dark place.
safety_notes.source_title: Water

safety_notes.text: Store at least 1 gallon per person per day for 3 days, and aim for 2 weeks if you can.
safety_notes.source_title: How to Create an Emergency Water Supply

safety_notes.text: Bottled water sold in the US is regulated by the FDA as a food, with rules on identity, quality limits for contaminants and manufacturing practice.
safety_notes.source_title: Bottled Water Everywhere: Keeping it Safe

safety_notes.text: Keep water away from direct sunlight and away from gasoline, pesticides and other toxic substances.

items.name: Bathtub water bladder
items.need: With a few hours' warning, a bladder turns the bathtub into a sealed tank of 65 to 100 gallons of clean tap water, filled before a storm, a freeze or an outage stops the taps.
items.how_to_choose: A bladder only helps if you fill it while the water is still running, so keep it in the bathroom and practice the steps once without filling it. Check that it fits your tub: a standard tub holds about 60 to 70 gallons, less than the headline number on the box. It is single-use in practice, because it cannot be dried out properly afterwards, and the tub is out of action while it is full. Buy a named brand from the maker or a known retailer and keep the hand pump with it.

qty.note: One per bathtub. No bathtub, no bladder: store more water in containers instead.

items.already_own: A clean bathtub filled directly holds water for flushing and washing, but an open tub is not a clean drinking-water container and a worn plug can leak it away overnight. If you already own a bladder, check that the liner, fill sleeve and pump are all in the box and that it has never been filled.

safety_notes.text: Plan on at least 1 gallon of water per person per day. A filled bathtub bladder can cover a household for many days, but it does not replace water stored in advance, because it only works if you get warning.
safety_notes.source_title: How to Create an Emergency Water Supply

items.name: Collapsible water carriers
items.need: If water is handed out at a street tanker, a hydrant station or a lower floor, someone has to carry it home and up the stairs, and soft carriers take almost no space until that day.
items.how_to_choose: Think in stair-loads, not gallons: 2.5 gallons (10 liters) weighs about 22 lb. On stairs carry one at a time, in one hand or on your back, so that a hand stays on the rail; two at once, one in each hand, is for level ground only. Bags that ride inside a backpack keep both hands free. Thin fold-flat cubes are cheap but crease and wear out; fabric-skinned bags last for years. Sanitize carriers before first use, and treat water from an uncertain source before drinking it.

qty.note: Two per household, a fixed number: two people can each carry one, or one person can make two trips. On stairs carry one at a time and keep a hand on the rail.

items.already_own: A hiking hydration bladder, a camping water cube or clean 2-liter soda bottles in a backpack all work. Check that the caps seal, the seams do not weep when squeezed full, and nothing smells musty after washing.

safety_notes.text: Before use, wash a container with soap, rinse, then sanitize with 1 teaspoon of unscented household bleach (5% to 9%) in 1 quart of water, shaking to wet all inside surfaces for at least 30 seconds before pouring it out.
safety_notes.source_title: How to Create an Emergency Water Supply

safety_notes.text: If you cannot be sure collected water is safe, boil it, or disinfect it with plain unscented bleach by the directions on its own label (U4-10). Boiling and bleach do not make water with fuel or toxic chemicals in it safe.
safety_notes.source_title: How to Make Water Safe in an Emergency

safety_notes.text: Use food-grade containers for drinking water and never one that has held toxic chemicals.

items.name: Spigots and pumps for water containers
items.need: A full container is too heavy to tip and pour without spilling, so you need a clean way to draw off a cup at a time.
items.how_to_choose: Match the dispenser to the container, because threads differ. The Rhino-Pak, this site's Standard container, pours from the spout it comes with and does not take the Reliance pump. The Aqua-Tainer, the Budget container, comes with a spigot and takes Reliance's 70 mm parts and its hand pump. A WaterBrick needs its own spigot lid, sold separately, and a Scepter military can pours from its small cap unless you buy its spout. With a 7-gallon can, which weighs about 60 lb full, the pump is worth buying: it lets the can stay upright on the floor instead of being lifted onto its side at a counter edge. With a lighter container, a spigot or spout that came with it and works is enough. A barrel with no spigot needs a siphon or barrel pump sold as food-grade, and a wrench for its bung. Keep hands and cups off the spout, and wash and sanitize dispenser parts when you clean the container.

qty.note: One working dispenser for the household, a fixed number. The spigot or spout that came with your container counts; buy a pump only if it fits that container, and keep a spare spigot if you rely on the original.

items.already_own: The spigot or spout that came with your container is enough if it seals and does not drip. Check it is not cracked and that the vent opens. Do not use a siphon or pump that has ever moved fuel or chemicals.

safety_notes.text: Clean and sanitize anything that touches stored drinking water: wash with soap, rinse, then use 1 teaspoon of unscented household bleach (5% to 9%) in 1 quart of water for at least 30 seconds.

safety_notes.text: Prefer containers with a narrow neck or opening and a tightly closing top, and never use equipment that has held toxic chemicals.
safety_notes.source_title: How to Create an Emergency Water Supply

item_flags: Many generic hand siphons and battery transfer pumps are sold for fuel as well as water: use only one sold as food-grade, and never one that has moved fuel.

budget.size: Fits Reliance containers with a 70 mm (2.75 in) opening made after 2015; includes spigot, cap, vent cap and vent plug
budget.price_seen_at: Reliance's own listing (relianceoutdoors.com), November 17, 2026; the maker's site is a catalog, so buy from a retailer
budget.why: An inexpensive spare for the spigot that comes with the Aqua-Tainer. The Prepared notes buyer reports of the white spigot and cap cracking with age, so a spare in the drawer keeps a 7-gallon can usable.
budget.weakness: It only fits Reliance's 70 mm containers (Aqua-Tainer, Aqua-Pak, Water-Pak, Jumbo-Tainer and similar), and the container still has to lie on its side at a counter edge to pour.

cadillac.size: Rechargeable tap-to-pour faucet, 2.7 x 6.7 x 6.1 in, 0.8 lb, about 40 gallons (150 L) per charge, magnetic base, hose with quick-connect fitting
cadillac.why: It works with any container, including the Rhino-Pak and the others the Reliance pump does not fit: drop the hose in, tap the top, and it pours a measured stream with one hand, then shuts off by itself. One charge moves about 40 gallons, and it has a small built-in light. GearJunkie's tester used one for over a year.
cadillac.weakness: It needs charging by USB, so keep it topped up and keep a manual spigot as a backup; its 23-inch hose will not reach the bottom of a tall barrel; and it is expensive for what is, in the end, a tap.
